items.title: OpenClaw: A Technical Overview
items.text:
OpenClaw is an open-source personal AI agent platform designed to function as a continuously running digital assistant rather than a traditional chatbot. Instead of simply answering questions, it is intended to observe, plan, interact with external systems, and execute multi-step tasks across applications and communication channels on behalf of a single user. (OpenClaw)

Unlike many AI products that live inside a web browser, OpenClaw is built around the idea that an assistant should exist as part of your computing environment—always available, persistent, and capable of interacting with your files, applications, messaging platforms, and online services.

For someone interested in operational systems and business infrastructure, OpenClaw is best thought of as an AI operating layer rather than simply another AI application.

items.title: Core Philosophy
items.text:
OpenClaw is built around several core principles:

  • Local-first operation
  • Persistent identity and memory
  • Cross-platform availability
  • Tool execution instead of conversation alone
  • User ownership of data and configuration
  • Extensible architecture through plugins and skills

Rather than opening ChatGPT every time work needs to be done, OpenClaw attempts to become a permanent operational assistant that can be reached from numerous interfaces while maintaining awareness of ongoing work. (OpenClaw)

items.title: Architecture Overview
items.text:
Conceptually, OpenClaw consists of several major layers.

User
 │
 │ WhatsApp / Telegram / Discord / Slack / CLI / Mobile App
 │
 ▼
OpenClaw Gateway
 │
 ├── Agent Runtime
 ├── Memory
 ├── Planner
 ├── Skills
 ├── Tool Execution
 ├── Model Provider
 │
 ▼
Computer + Cloud Services

The Gateway serves as the central control plane, routing requests, maintaining agent state, and coordinating actions across external services. Companion mobile applications provide monitoring and control rather than hosting the AI themselves. (OpenClaw)

items.title: Communication Channels
items.text:
One of OpenClaw's defining characteristics is that it communicates through platforms people already use.

Supported integrations include:

  • WhatsApp
  • Telegram
  • Slack
  • Discord
  • Signal
  • Microsoft Teams
  • Google Chat
  • Matrix
  • iMessage
  • IRC
  • LINE
  • WeChat
  • Mattermost
  • Twitch
  • Synology Chat
  • and many others. (GitHub)

This allows the assistant to be accessed from nearly anywhere without requiring a dedicated interface.

Examples include:

  • sending yourself reminders
  • asking for project status
  • requesting report generation
  • approving agent actions
  • checking calendars
  • retrieving documents

items.title: Skills
items.text:
One of OpenClaw's most important concepts is the Skill.

A Skill is a self-contained capability that teaches the agent how to perform a specific category of work.

Examples might include:

  • GitHub automation
  • invoice processing
  • email drafting
  • CRM lookup
  • filesystem search
  • document generation
  • API interaction
  • database queries

Skills are stored independently from the core engine, allowing new capabilities to be added without modifying the underlying system. The workspace convention uses dedicated skill folders containing structured instructions. (GitHub)

items.title: Persistent Memory
items.text:
Unlike stateless chat sessions, OpenClaw maintains persistent information about:

  • previous conversations
  • user preferences
  • project context
  • installed skills
  • configuration
  • workspace state

This persistence enables the assistant to continue long-running work over days or weeks instead of treating every interaction as a fresh conversation. (GitHub)

items.title: Workspace
items.text:
Each OpenClaw installation has its own workspace.

Typical contents include:

workspace/

    AGENTS.md
    SOUL.md
    TOOLS.md

    skills/

    projects/

    notes/

    documents/

The workspace acts as the assistant's operational environment.

It stores:

  • instructions
  • operational rules
  • memory
  • documents
  • reusable prompts
  • project data

OpenClaw injects files such as AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, and TOOLS.md into the agent context to shape behavior. (GitHub)

items.title: Agent Personalities
items.text:
One of OpenClaw's distinguishing features is its use of structured behavioral guidance.

Instead of relying solely on prompts typed into a chat window, behavior can be encoded in files describing:

  • communication style
  • responsibilities
  • limitations
  • objectives
  • operational rules
  • decision boundaries

This is conceptually similar to the "company characters" and control-folder approach you have been developing for your own documentation, where behavior is defined by structured files rather than ephemeral prompts.

items.title: Tool Execution
items.text:
OpenClaw is designed to perform actions, not merely generate text.

Depending on installed integrations, it can:

  • read files
  • write files
  • search folders
  • execute shell commands
  • call APIs
  • interact with Git repositories
  • manage calendars
  • send emails
  • schedule reminders
  • automate repetitive workflows

This moves it closer to an autonomous software operator than a conversational assistant. (OpenClaw)

items.title: Multi-Model Support
items.text:
OpenClaw is model-agnostic.

Rather than being tied to one provider, it can work with multiple model backends, allowing users to choose the provider and model that best fit their needs. Documentation recommends configuring the provider and model in the local configuration file. (GitHub)

Potential use cases include:

  • GPT models
  • Claude models
  • Gemini models
  • locally hosted models
  • future providers

This separation between orchestration and inference makes the platform adaptable as AI models evolve.

items.title: Long-Running Agents
items.text:
Unlike browser chats that terminate when the window closes, OpenClaw is intended to run continuously as a background service.

The onboarding process can install the Gateway as a user service so it remains active after login. (GitHub)

That enables capabilities such as:

  • watching directories
  • responding to incoming messages
  • scheduled automation
  • recurring reporting
  • proactive notifications

items.title: Development Environment
items.text:
OpenClaw is built primarily around modern JavaScript tooling.

Typical development components include:

  • Node.js
  • pnpm
  • npm
  • Git
  • GitHub

It runs on:

  • Linux
  • macOS
  • Windows (typically through WSL2)

Developers can install from packages or clone the full source repository. (OpenClaw)

items.title: Extensibility
items.text:
OpenClaw is intentionally designed as a platform rather than a finished application.

Developers can extend it by creating:

  • new Skills
  • new communication channels
  • model providers
  • automation routines
  • tool integrations
  • workspace conventions

The architecture isolates integrations and providers from the core runtime, making it easier to add capabilities without changing the central agent loop. (Reddit)

items.title: Security Considerations
items.text:
Because OpenClaw can operate with broad access to local files, messaging platforms, and external services, security is a major consideration.

Potential risks include:

  • excessive filesystem permissions
  • malicious or compromised skills
  • prompt injection through untrusted content
  • supply-chain vulnerabilities in plugins
  • unintended execution of privileged actions

Recent research has highlighted that persistent memory, tool execution, and high-privilege integrations expand the attack surface compared with conventional chatbots, emphasizing the need for permission boundaries, trusted skills, and careful configuration. (arXiv)

items.title: Where OpenClaw Fits
items.text:
OpenClaw occupies a space between several familiar categories:

Traditional Software OpenClaw Equivalent ChatGPT Persistent personal assistant Automation scripts Intelligent workflow orchestration Task scheduler AI-driven execution engine CLI utilities Natural-language control interface Personal knowledge base Persistent memory system Workflow automation Autonomous agent platform

Rather than replacing existing software, it acts as a coordinating layer that can invoke those tools, maintain context, and automate multi-step tasks.

For technically inclined users—particularly those building operational systems, automation workflows, or AI-enabled business infrastructure—OpenClaw provides a framework for creating a continuously running assistant that can bridge messaging platforms, development tools, local resources, and cloud services while remaining under the user's control. (OpenClaw)

For more information, see the official OpenClaw website and the OpenClaw GitHub repository.

items.title: AI Control System
items.text:
This resource — a project website and its collection of files — is operated by people and AI agents together. Because everything here is plain Markdown, an agent reads the same files a person does.

A control system is the small set of Markdown files that tell an agent how to work on this resource: how to understand it, run it, extend it, and maintain it — along with the rules to follow, the current build recipe, the history of changes, and the open work. It is the governance layer, kept deliberately separate from the site's actual content, so an agent always has a reliable place to learn the "rules of the house" before making changes.

items.text:

items.title: How to Rebuild & Run (Zensical)
items.text:
This site is built with Zensical, run from an isolated Python virtual environment at .venv/. Use that environment's zensical, not a system-wide install.

All commands run from the project root:

/home/morgen/Documents/Vaults/morgen/abs-future/zensical-abs-1

items.title: Everyday routine
items.text:
Author and publish through the ./build.sh wrapper, run from the project root. It does two things the raw zensical commands do not: regenerate the nav (so new pages appear in the sidebar) and, for publishing, encrypt every page. build.sh uses the project's .venv internally, so there's no venv to activate.

./build.sh serve     # regenerate nav → live preview at http://localhost:8000 (Ctrl-C to stop)
./build.sh deploy    # regenerate nav → build → encrypt → push to GitHub Pages

Use ./build.sh serve while writing: it regenerates the blog-style nav first, so pages you just created with ./new-entry actually show up in the left-nav.

items.title: What each command does
items.text:
Command What it's for ./build.sh serve Authoring preview. Regenerates the nav, then live-reloads at :8000. Use this while writing. ./build.sh deploy Publish. Regenerate nav → build → AES-encrypt every page → force-push to the gh-pages branch. ./build.sh Build + encrypt into site/ locally, no push — e.g. to inspect the protected output. zensical serve (raw) Quick engine-only preview. Skips nav regeneration, so new ./new-entry pages won't appear — prefer ./build.sh serve. Needs the venv (source .venv/bin/activate or prefix ./.venv/bin/). zensical build (raw) Raw compile to site/, unencrypted — never host or deploy this directly.

To view it: run ./build.sh serve, then open http://localhost:8000.

Why the wrapper? The nav is a generated list and every published page is password-encrypted. Raw zensical serve/build do neither — they drop new entries from the nav and (for build) emit plaintext. ./build.sh adds those two steps, so it's the reliable path for both previewing and publishing.

items.title: First-time / recreate the environment
items.text:
Only needed if .venv/ is missing or on a new machine:

cd /home/morgen/Documents/Vaults/morgen/abs-future/zensical-abs-1
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip zensical

Zensical bundles its theme, search, and Markdown processing, so there is no long plugin list to install — a deliberate contrast with the MkDocs hub, whose ~14 plugins are documented in that project's own setup docs.

items.title: Site Adjustments — Change Journal (Zensical build)
items.text: Chronological log of notable changes to this Zensical site. Append newest entries at the top. This is the "what changed and why"; the "how it works now" lives in site-setup-and-settings.md.

• Extended blog-style sections to Challenges + Timeline; generalized the nav script. Renamed gen-meetings-nav.py → scripts/gen-blog-nav.py, now driven by a BLOG_SECTIONS list (Meetings, Challenges, Timeline); each folder's index.md (if present) leads, then entries newest-first, spliced between per-section # >>> NAME … <<< markers. Challenges (business-challenges/) is now a blog folder (kept its index landing; tab moved to right of Phases). Timeline is a new top-level section (right of Meetings): renamed from Work's timeline.md → timeline/index.md landing + dated entries, each carrying tags: front matter. Tags render as chips out of the box (verified) — no config, no plugin; there is no built-in tags index page (declined for now). Added templates/timeline.md and templates/challenge.md.

  • Added a "Meetings" blog-like section (top-level tab, newest-first). Converted the stale single meeting-notes.md into docs/work/meetings/, one dated .md per meeting (YYYY-MM-DD-topic.md). Added scripts/gen-meetings-nav.py, run by build.sh (step 0), which scans the folder and rewrites the Meetings nav list newest-first between # >>> MEETINGS … <<< markers in zensical.toml (folder auto-include only sorts ascending, so a script is needed for reverse order). "Meetings" is its own top nav tab after "Work"; nav labels come from each entry's H1. Enabled navigation.expand so the sidebar opens expanded. Added templates/meeting.md to copy for new entries. Workflow: copy the template to a dated file in meetings/, then ./build.sh deploy.

  • Added two diagram sub-pages under the Project Hub landing. personal-picture.md (Personal → Local → Group → Intelligence) and business-picture.md (Operations & Automation Journey), images in docs/images/. Converted the home nav entry from a bare index.md to a { "Project Hub" = [index.md, personal-picture.md, business-picture.md] } section so the two pages nest under the landing. Each image is click-to-open at full size (no glightbox in Zensical). Note: mapped by content — business diagram → "Business Picture", personal diagram → "Personal Picture".

  • Added the ABS logo + favicon. Pulled the official logo from absolutebusinesssupply.ca into docs/images/ (colored logo-color.png, white logo-white.png, and favicon.png). Set [project.theme] logo = "images/logo-color.png" and favicon = "images/favicon.png". Chose the colored logo because Zensical's "modern" header uses a light background (--md-default-bg-color--light), where the white logo would be invisible. Caveat: the colored (dark) logo is faint in dark/slate mode; logo-white.png is staged for a light/dark swap if wanted.

  • Fixed per-page password prompts → single unlock for the whole site. Root cause: build.sh passed -c false to staticrypt, which suppressed the persistent salt config — every page got its own salt, so the localStorage "remember me" key never matched on the next page. Fix: generated a project-root .staticrypt.json (one shared salt, embedded in all 42 pages), removed -c false, set --remember 365, and post-processed the prompt so the "Remember me" checkbox is ticked by default. Result: enter the password once → stored (salted+hashed) in localStorage → every other page auto-decrypts silently. Verified: shared salt present in 42/42 built pages, checked on all prompts, no plaintext/password in output.

  • Search kept ON (accepted trade-off). search.json is served unencrypted, so it's directly fetchable by URL — a low-severity content-disclosure risk accepted for this non-sensitive site (the UI shows only the password box until unlocked, so there's no usable search box pre-unlock). build.sh documents a one-line opt-out to drop the index if that ever changes.
  • Deployed to GitHub Pages. Created public repo peers8862/abs-project-hub-zensical holding only the encrypted gh-pages branch (same model as the MkDocs hub — source and password stay local). Live at https://peers8862.github.io/abs-project-hub-zensical/ with .nojekyll.

• Added password protection (staticrypt). Since Zensical has no encryptcontent equivalent, build.sh now runs staticrypt over the built site/ as a post-build step — AES-encrypting every page + injecting a password prompt. Password comes from a gitignored .env (SITE_PASSWORD); the build fails closed if it's missing. Disabled navigation.instant/.prefetch (incompatible with per-page encryption). Verified: all 41 pages encrypted, no plaintext content or password in site/, guard aborts without the password. Caveat: the search index is left unencrypted (opt-out one-liner in build.sh); the client-side model isn't vault-grade.
  • Added hub/company-doc enhancements (Tier 1 + 2), all plugin-free. Home page → branded grid-card hub; division-of-duties-maps.md and automation-inventory.md → native Mermaid diagrams; Proposed → task-list + status table board; First Focus → content tabs (Remote/In-Person). Added a site-wide glossary: docs/includes/abbreviations.md is auto-appended via pymdownx.snippets, so acronyms render as hover tooltips everywhere. Enabled custom_dir = "overrides" and added overrides/main.html with a dismissible announcement bar ({% block announce %}). Brand-tinted card hover + banner via stylesheets/extra.css. Verified: clean zensical build; grid/banner/mermaid/tabbed/task-list/abbr all present in site/. Deferred: page status badges — Zensical has no icon.status front-matter wiring yet (the md-status CSS ships, but the config hook doesn't). Revisit later.
  • Enabled top navigation tabs. Added "navigation.tabs" to [project.theme].features in zensical.toml, so the 10 top-level sections render as a tab bar across the header (on viewports ≥ 1220px; collapses to the drawer on mobile). Verified: md-tabs bar renders all 10 section labels. Note: sticky tabs (navigation.tabs.sticky) are available in Zensical open-source — unlike Material for MkDocs, where they're Insiders-only.
  • Initial Zensical build — migrated content + navigation from the MkDocs hub. Copied all content sections (orientation, phases, work, business-challenges, roadmap-ideas, site-family, prices, refs) and the steel-blue brand CSS from the sibling mkdocs-projecthub1 site into docs/. Verified: zensical build succeeds and zensical serve renders the full navigation.
  • Translated navigation from awesome-pages to a central nav array. The MkDocs hub used a .pages file per folder; those were converted into one explicit nav = [...] in zensical.toml, preserving custom section titles ("Sites?", "Spokes", "Phase One: Driver's Seat", etc.) and page order. The .pages files were dropped (Zensical ignores them).
  • Adapted the AI control section for Zensical. Rewrote every docs/ai/ page to describe the Zensical build (commands, config, extensions, module-system status) instead of the MkDocs tooling. Adopted a single-source model — the control docs live only under docs/ai/, with no mirrored root-level copies.
  • Dropped MkDocs-only features. Password protection (encryptcontent), image lightbox (glightbox), page dates (git-revision-date), and macros/mkdocstrings/ redirects/minify — none have a Zensical equivalent yet. See extensions-and-modules.md.
  • Handled the work/proposed split. The MkDocs hub had both a work/proposed.md file and a work/proposed/ folder; the "Proposed" spine page became work/proposed/index.md (the section landing) with first-focus.md beneath it.

The Zensical build of the ABS Project Hub — a static documentation site built with Zensical, authored in plain Markdown, with content migrated from the sibling MkDocs hub. It is a parallel evaluation site: the MkDocs hub remains the protected, deployed source of truth for now.

Stack: Zensical 0.0.x · Python 3.11 in a .venv/ · centralized nav in zensical.toml · steel-blue brand. No password gate (Zensical has no encryptcontent equivalent — see §5).

items.title: 1. Prerequisites
items.text:
• Python 3.11+ with venv
  • git and (for deployment) the GitHub CLI (gh)

items.title: 2. Create the project + environment
items.text:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip zensical
zensical new .          # scaffold (already done for this project)

.gitignore should exclude .venv/ and /site/.

items.title: 3. Configuration (zensical.toml)
items.text:
Zensical uses a single TOML config. Key sections:

  • [project] — site_name, site_description, site_author, copyright, and the explicit nav array (see §4).
  • [project.theme] — features (navigation.*, content.*, search.highlight), language, and [[project.theme.palette]] blocks for the light/dark toggle.
  • [project.markdown_extensions.*] — the enabled extensions (see extensions-and-modules.md).
  • extra_css = ["stylesheets/extra.css"] — loads the steel-blue brand color.

items.title: 4. Content structure & navigation
items.text:
• Folders = sidebar sections; .md files = pages. A folder's index.md is its landing page (navigation.indexes).
  • Navigation is centralized in zensical.toml as an explicit nav array — there are no per-folder .pages files. TOML shape: 
    nav = [
  "index.md",
  { "Phases" = [
      "phases/index.md",
      { "Phase One: Driver's Seat" = [ "phases/phase-one/index.md", "phases/phase-one/get-fluent.md" ] },
  ] },
]
  • The first # Heading in a file is its page title.

Top-level sections (titles set in the nav array): Home, Sites?, Phases, Work, Challenges, Docs, Spokes, Prices, Refs, AI.

items.title: 5. Password protection — staticrypt (client-side gate)
items.text:
Zensical has no in-build encryption (no plugin system → no encryptcontent). Protection is a post-build step: build.sh runs staticrypt over the built site/, AES-encrypting every page and injecting a password prompt — the same client-side model the MkDocs hub used.

  • Password source: the gitignored .env (SITE_PASSWORD). build.sh loads it and fails closed if it's missing, so an unprotected site is never produced.
  • Build & protect: ./build.sh builds then encrypts into site/. ./build.sh serve gives a local unencrypted preview for authoring (never deployed).
  • Compatibility: navigation.instant/.prefetch are disabled in zensical.toml — staticrypt replaces each page's HTML, which instant-nav (SPA fetches) can't consume.
  • Security model: client-side only — encrypted content + derived key reach the browser, so it's good against the public, not vault-grade (offline brute-forceable). For stronger protection, host behind Cloudflare Access.
  • Known gap: the search index is copied unencrypted, so search can expose page text. build.sh has a commented one-liner to drop it if that matters.
  • Verify before publishing: grep -rl '<password>' site | wc -l → 0, and a known content phrase must NOT appear in the encrypted HTML.

items.title: 6. Deployment — GitHub Pages via Actions
items.text:
The scaffold includes .github/workflows/docs.yml, which on push to master/main runs zensical build --clean and deploys site/ to GitHub Pages via the official Pages actions. To enable:

  1. git init and create a GitHub repo for this project.
  2. Push to master/main; enable Pages (source: GitHub Actions) in repo settings.

(Not yet wired — this project is currently local-only.)

items.title: Creating New Posts in Standard way
items.text: We're creating a small local command-line tool — scripts/new_entry.py, run via a ./new-entry wrapper — that scaffolds new pages for your Zensical site from templates. Today the workflow is manual (copy a template, rename it with the date, open your editor); the tool collapses that into one command that handles the filename, date, and template-filling for you. It's written in Python (matching your existing gen-blog-nav.py), uses only the standard library, and runs from your project's .venv. It writes the correctly-named .md file into the right folder; your next ./build.sh picks it up and slots it into the nav automatically.

items.title: The two modes and how collisions work
items.text: It runs in two modes. Scaffold mode (the default) asks you 2–3 quick questions, stamps the template, writes the file, and drops you into your editor (Sublime via subl, falling back to $EDITOR, then nano) to write the prose. Fill mode (--fill) does the same but first walks each section at the terminal, prompting you for its content — the mechanic there is plain Enter only: Enter after typing text = next bullet/line, Enter on an empty line = finish that section and move on (no Ctrl+Enter, since terminals can't detect it). The template itself decides whether a section takes bullets or prose. If a filename already exists (same date + title), it appends a word-form suffix — -TWO, -THREE, up to -TEN — to the file and a matching (TWO) to the heading so the nav stays distinct.

items.title: The eight template types and how you operate it
items.text: The tool offers eight doc types: [1] Challenge (Business Challenges → docs/business-challenges/, the 7-section template), [2] Meeting (Agenda · Decisions · Action items · Actions taken → docs/work/meetings/), [3] Call (Topics · Observations · Insights · Suggested actions → docs/work/calls/), [4] Idea (Topic · Summary · Connections · Contexts → docs/ideas/), [5] Reference (Description · Link → docs/refs/), [6] Timeline (a single prose body → docs/timeline/), [7] Automation (Overview · Trigger · Steps · Systems & tools · Intended impact · Business considerations → docs/automations/), and [8] Operation (Business area · Current approach · AI & agent enhancement · Depth & reach gained · Considerations → docs/operations/). To operate it, run ./new-entry (or ./new-entry --fill), pick the type by number, type a title, press Enter to accept today's date (or type your own), and the tool writes the file and opens it for you — with fill mode, you answer each section prompt at the terminal first. All eight sections are wired into the site's left-nav (newest-first), so new pages appear in navigation on the next ./build.sh.

items.title: What kind of site is this?
items.text:
There is a class of open-source website systems built for documenting company processes — freely downloadable packages that provide the bones and the logic for document-based sites meant for staff and partners, not customers or the public.

We can re-purpose these to create persistent long-term references for the partners as well as temporary, project- or training-focused sites. This hub — the Project Site — is the home base. It links out to the rest of the site family.

This project-hub site is made using an open website system named Zensical. It's a successor to the very popular "Material for MKDocs" project that's dedicated to free documentation sites.

Site currently hosted on Morgen's personal github account under a repo named abs-project-hub-zensical. When the site is visited in a browser it is password protected. The files published to the Github repo do not reveal the password. If we continue, recommendations will be given on more sustainable and secure approaches to creating sites.

Every site in this class:

  • Serves human readers and AI agents equally — people read the pages, agents scan the same source files, guided by their own control folders
  • Is a static site you can view locally (no internet required) or host cheaply and reliably
  • Is built from Markdown — the same format all AI agent systems rely on — so any research doc, report, or summary either partner creates can be dropped straight into a folder and it becomes a page

Start with How these sites work, then Git, GitHub & privacy.

items.title: For AI Agents (Control Folders)
items.text:
Every site here serves agents as well as people. Where the published pages are for human readers, agents are steered by dedicated control folders — collections of guidance and behavior files ("company characters") that tell an agent how to read the source files, what routines to run, and what standard outputs to produce.

Below is a general introduction to the broad concept of "harnesses for AI". Every project and business division requires different kinds of tailored control systems but there are general principles that guide these different situations.

items.title: For AI Agents (Control Folders)
items.text:
This section describes the machine-facing layer of the system. It exists in parallel with the human-readable documentation but operates under a different set of constraints: determinism, consistency, and explicit behavioral control.

The site is not only a collection of pages. It is also a structured environment for agents to read, reason over, and write into.

Human users interact with rendered content. Agents interact with control folders and structured instructions.

items.title: For AI Agents (Control Folders)
items.text:
This section describes the machine-facing layer of the system. It exists in parallel with the human-readable documentation but operates under a different set of constraints: determinism, consistency, and explicit behavioral control.

The site is not only a collection of pages. It is also a structured environment for agents to read, reason over, and write into.

Human users interact with rendered content. Agents interact with control folders and structured instructions.

items.title: 1. System Overview
items.text:
Each site in this hub is composed of two coupled layers:

  • Content Layer (Human-facing)
  • Markdown pages, guides, explanations, references
  • Designed for readability and exploration

  • May be incomplete, narrative, or interpretive

  • Control Layer (Agent-facing)

  • Structured folders containing operational instructions
  • Deterministic rules for reading, transformation, and writing
  • Defines boundaries of action and expected output formats

Agents do not treat these layers as equivalent. The control layer has precedence when interpreting intent.

items.title: 2. Control Folder Convention
items.text:
Each site includes one or more control folders. These folders define how agents should behave within that site.

Typical structure:

/control/ agent.md permissions.md workflows/ schemas/ outputs/ memory/

items.title: Core principles
items.text:
• Control folders are explicitly machine-targeted
  • They are not prose documentation
  • They define:
  • Allowed operations
  • Input interpretation rules
  • Output formatting standards
  • Cross-file reading strategy

items.title: Naming rules
items.text:
• control/ is the canonical root name (may be nested per subsystem)
  • Subfolders are domain-scoped (e.g. billing/, docs/, agents/)
  • Files should be single-responsibility and stable over time

items.title: 3. Agent Binding to a Site
items.text:
An agent is considered attached to a site when it is given:

  • A root directory path
  • A control-folder entrypoint (usually control/agent.md)
  • A declared permission scope (read-only or read-write subsets)

From this entrypoint, the agent constructs its operational model:

  1. Load control instructions first
  2. Parse available schemas and workflows
  3. Index readable content folders
  4. Determine write boundaries
  5. Begin task execution within constraints

Agents are not assumed to understand the site globally. They reconstruct it from the control layer.

items.title: 4. Company Characters (Behavior Profiles)
items.text:
Within the control layer, company characters define consistent behavioral roles.

A company character is not a persona. It is a constraint bundle.

Each character defines:

  • Interpretation style of ambiguous instructions
  • Preferred output structure
  • Validation rules before writing files
  • Error handling strategy
  • Level of autonomy allowed

Example roles:

  • Indexer Character
  • Focuses on reading and structuring existing content
  • Avoids writing unless explicitly required

  • Prioritizes completeness

  • Builder Character

  • Produces structured artifacts
  • Follows schemas strictly

  • Minimizes narrative output

  • Maintainer Character

  • Edits and refines existing files
  • Preserves structure and reduces drift

  • Applies consistency rules

  • Synthesizer Character

  • Combines multiple sources into derived outputs
  • Creates summaries or indexes
  • Must reference sources explicitly

Characters may be assigned statically or dynamically per workflow.

items.title: 5. Read and Write Discipline
items.text: Agents treat the filesystem as a controlled state machine.

items.title: Read rules
items.text:
• Read control instructions before content
  • Prefer structured files over narrative pages
  • Do not infer missing rules from content
  • Resolve conflicts in favor of control layer

items.title: Write rules
items.text:
• Outputs must conform to declared schemas
  • New files must declare origin context in metadata
  • Edits must preserve structure unless explicitly overridden
  • No writing outside defined output directories

items.title: 6. Workflows
items.text:
Workflows define repeatable operational sequences.

Typical elements:

  • Trigger condition
  • Required inputs
  • Transformation steps
  • Output targets
  • Validation rules

Examples:

  • Indexing folder trees
  • Converting raw notes into structured documentation
  • Syncing control and content layers
  • Performing consistency audits

Workflows are explicit to prevent emergent or implicit behavior.

items.title: 7. Output Propagation
items.text:
Outputs are not final until placed in designated zones:

  • /outputs/ for transient artifacts
  • /docs/ for stable documentation
  • /generated/ for raw machine output

Rules:

  • Outputs may be re-ingested by later runs
  • Human edits override machine outputs unless revalidated
  • Control changes may invalidate prior outputs

items.title: 8. State, Memory, and Continuity
items.text:
Agents maintain no implicit runtime memory.

Continuity is achieved through:

  • Control files
  • Persistent outputs
  • Explicit state artifacts

There is no assumption of persistent execution context.

items.title: 9. Safety and Boundaries
items.text:
Agents operate under strict constraints:

  • No modification outside declared write zones
  • No execution of undefined workflows
  • No generation of control logic unless permitted
  • No silent restructuring of control folders

Design principle: predictable limitation over autonomy.

items.title: 10. Extension Point
items.text:
This section is intentionally open.

Future additions may include:

  • Formal schema definitions
  • Inter-agent communication protocols
  • Verification layers for outputs
  • Multi-agent coordination models
  • External system integrations

items.title: Git, GitHub & Privacy
items.text: These sites can live purely on your own computer, but they get far more useful once Git and GitHub are in the picture.

items.title: What Git is
items.text:
Git is a system for tracking changes to files over time. Think of it like a very detailed "save history" for a project. Instead of only having the latest version of a document, Git keeps snapshots of how everything looked at different points in time — so you can go back, compare changes, or see exactly who changed what and when. It's especially useful when several people work on the same project, because it helps prevent people from accidentally overwriting each other's work.

It works by storing these snapshots in a structured way called a "repository." When someone makes changes, they "commit" them — like taking a new snapshot with a note explaining what changed. These commits form a timeline that can branch in different directions, then merge back together once the best version is chosen.

For our purposes: partners and assistants can develop or evolve materials separately, then — with Git's help — humans or AI agents oversee the merge, handing everyone back one unified copy of the file collection.

items.title: What GitHub adds
items.text: GitHub is the main global site where programmers warehouse code, but anyone can use it. Because it's built for advanced technical users, its settings and its integration with hundreds of desktop tools are unmatched. This project uses GitHub's free, reliable hosting to serve readable sites.

items.title: Privacy
items.text:
These sites are readable and non-interactive by default. Password protection is an option where a site should stay private to the partners rather than public.

Access model — to decide per site

Some sites in the family are naturally public-safe (e.g. general training material); others (administration, sales relationships) should stay private. We'll set the access level as each site takes shape.

items.title: How These Sites Work
items.text: You don't need to be technical to add to this site. The whole system is just folders and Markdown files.

items.title: The core idea
items.text:
• Folders are sections. Each folder in the site becomes a section heading in the left-hand sidebar.
  • Markdown files are pages. Drop a .md file into a folder and it shows up as a page in that section the next time the site loads.
  • The first heading is the page title. Start a file with # My Title and that becomes its name in the sidebar.

That means adding a report, a summary, or a set of meeting notes is as simple as saving a .md file into the right folder — no menus to edit, no code to write.

If you don't add one, pages simply appear in alphabetical order. You can rename or reorder anything later without breaking links.

items.title: Viewing the site
items.text:
• Locally: run the site and open it in your browser — no internet needed.
  • Shared: the same files can be published so both partners (and agents) see one unified copy. See Git, GitHub & privacy.

Markdown is the shared language

Markdown is also the format AI agents read and write. So a file you write by hand and a file an agent produces are the same kind of thing — both slot into these folders and both become pages.

items.title: Operational Layer (Systems That Persist Beyond Training)
items.text: This part of the work focuses on building repeatable structures rather than one-off knowledge transfer. The aim is to leave behind systems that continue to operate, generate outputs, and coordinate work after the initial setup phase.

items.title: AI Environments & “Company Characters”
items.text:
AI is treated as an operational layer inside the organisation rather than a tool used ad hoc. This is implemented through structured agent environments built directly into project folders.

Each environment contains “company characters” — defined sets of behavioural rules expressed as guidance files. These are not personas; they are constrained operational roles that shape how an agent reads inputs, produces outputs, and enforces consistency.

In practice this means:

  • Folder-based agent definitions that encode roles, boundaries, and routines
  • Standardised behaviour across tasks regardless of execution context
  • Repeatable outputs that reduce reliance on individual interpretation or memory
  • Clear separation between human intent and machine execution logic

The result is a system where work is not only performed, but performed in a consistent and inspectable way.

items.title: Prompt Library (Reusable Knowledge Layer)
items.text:
A structured index of prompts is created as a shared operational resource.

This functions as a reusable execution layer for common tasks, including analysis, communication, reporting, and tool-based workflows.

Key characteristics:

  • Centralised storage of tested prompts
  • Fast retrieval and reuse across multiple contexts
  • Reduction of duplicated cognitive effort
  • Standardisation of output quality across team members and sessions

Over time, this becomes a compounding asset: a growing library of proven instructions that can be injected into workflows rather than recreated.

items.title: Scripts & Scheduled Workflows
items.text:
Local scripts and scheduled routines are installed on each participant’s machine to anchor daily and weekly operations.

These are designed to make work visible, structured, and synchronised without requiring manual coordination overhead.

Core functions include:

  • Automatic capture of ongoing work state
  • Standardised recording of tasks and outputs
  • Lightweight synchronisation between partners’ activity streams
  • Continuous visibility of progress without manual reporting

This creates a shared operational rhythm where work is continuously surfaced rather than periodically compiled.

items.title: Session Model Integration
items.text:
These systems are not built in isolation. They are embedded directly into working sessions.

Each session alternates between:

  • Practical training in tools and workflows
  • Direct construction of live systems inside the business context

This ensures that every engagement produces something operational — not just understanding, but infrastructure that continues to function after the session ends.

items.title: Phase Two: Building the Systems a $5–20M Business Needs
items.text:
Phase One makes the owners capable. Phase Two makes the business capable of running leaner as it grows — each step incremental, but moving fast enough to matter. The throughline: every dollar of new revenue is absorbed by better systems first, a new hire only as a last resort.

  • Local AI Hardware — speed, privacy, no per-use cost
  • Secure Chat Agents — coordination on Telegram / WhatsApp
  • Virtual-Employee Agents — work that would otherwise need a hire

items.title: On-Device AI Models (Local Execution Layer)
items.text:
A portion of AI workloads is shifted from cloud-hosted systems to on-device or locally hosted models. The objective is to optimise for speed, privacy, and operational independence while maintaining consistent performance for routine tasks.

This layer is not a replacement for external models, but a selective routing strategy: repetitive, predictable, or sensitive operations are executed locally, while heavier or more exploratory tasks can still be delegated to cloud systems when required.

Local execution becomes increasingly important as AI usage scales across daily workflows, because it prevents cost and dependency from growing linearly with usage.

items.title: Core Rationale
items.text:
On-device models introduce three structural advantages:

  • Latency reduction
  • Requests are executed locally without network round-trips
  • Predictable response times for routine workflows

  • Useful for interactive or frequently repeated tasks

  • Cost stability

  • Removes per-call or per-token billing for high-volume operations
  • Shifts cost from usage-based to infrastructure-based

  • Prevents AI usage from scaling into an unpredictable operating expense

  • Data containment

  • Sensitive operational data remains within local environments
  • Reduces exposure through external APIs or third-party processing layers
  • Supports compliance and internal control requirements

items.title: Why it matters for ABS
items.text:
Within the ABS operating context, this layer directly supports both operational efficiency and risk reduction:

  • No metered per-use billing for high-volume routine tasks such as summarisation, formatting, classification, or template generation
  • Customer, pricing, and internal operational data remain within controlled environments rather than being transmitted externally
  • Systems remain functional under degraded or unreliable connectivity, ensuring continuity of basic operations
  • Enables predictable scaling of AI usage without proportional increases in external service cost

items.title: Practical Usage Pattern
items.text:
In practice, workloads are divided into tiers:

  • Local tier
  • Repetitive transformations
  • Structured data processing
  • Template-based generation

  • Routine summarisation and formatting

  • External tier

  • Complex reasoning or multi-step synthesis
  • Large-scale analysis beyond local model capacity
  • Tasks requiring broader contextual knowledge

This separation ensures that local systems handle the majority of operational load while external systems are used selectively where they provide clear additional value.

items.title: Operational Effect
items.text:
As AI becomes embedded into more parts of the workflow, local execution functions as a stabilising layer:

  • Cost remains bounded even as usage increases
  • Core workflows continue independently of external service availability
  • Sensitive operational data is not routinely exposed outside the organisation
  • Day-to-day AI operations become more deterministic and controllable over time

items.title: Private Chat Agents (Messaging Layer)
items.text:
Private chat agents are deployed inside existing messaging platforms such as Telegram and WhatsApp, forming a lightweight operational interface for both internal coordination and, later, selective customer interaction.

Rather than introducing a new system that requires training or adoption, this approach embeds AI functionality directly into communication channels that are already part of daily behaviour. The intent is to reduce friction at the point of use while increasing the speed at which operational questions can be resolved.

The initial deployment is strictly internal, focused on enabling partners and team members to access structured business information, trigger simple workflows, and coordinate activity without leaving chat-based environments.

Over time, this same interface can be selectively extended outward to customers, but only where reliability and clarity of responses are already proven internally.

items.title: Core Design Intent
items.text:
This layer is not positioned as a chatbot layer in the traditional sense. It is closer to a queryable operational surface over existing systems.

Its design priorities are:

  • Minimise context switching during daily operations
  • Provide immediate access to structured business data
  • Reduce dependency on dashboards or manual lookups
  • Maintain strict control over what information is exposed and to whom
  • Allow incremental expansion from internal use to external-facing services

The emphasis is on controlled utility rather than open-ended conversation.

items.title: Internal Use Case (Phase 1)
items.text:
In the initial phase, private chat agents act as internal assistants embedded within partner communication channels.

Typical interactions include:

  • “What is the current stock level for item X?”
  • “What price did we last quote this customer?”
  • “What is the status of order Y?”
  • “Summarise recent activity on account Z”
  • “Log or retrieve operational notes tied to a project or customer”

These queries are resolved by connecting chat input to structured backend systems and returning concise, actionable outputs.

This removes the need to open separate tools or dashboards for routine operational questions.

items.title: Why it matters for ABS
items.text:
Within the ABS system, this layer plays a bridging role between structured infrastructure and day-to-day execution.

Key benefits:

  • Meets the team where they already operate
  • No behavioural change required to begin using AI-assisted workflows

  • Reduces resistance to adoption by embedding into familiar tools

  • Instant operational visibility

  • Internal agents can respond to questions about stock levels, pricing history, order status, or project state without delay

  • Reduces time spent searching across systems or asking others for updates

  • Reduced coordination overhead

  • Replaces repetitive status-checking conversations with direct queries

  • Creates a shared, consistent source of truth accessible through chat

  • Controlled path to external automation

  • Internal usage establishes reliability patterns, error handling, and trust boundaries
  • Only after stabilisation are customer-facing chat agents introduced
  • Prevents premature exposure of unfinished automation logic to external users

items.title: System Role in the Broader Stack
items.text:
Private chat agents sit between structured data systems and human coordination layers.

They function as:

  • A natural-language interface to operational systems
  • A lightweight orchestration layer for simple workflows
  • A feedback channel for understanding what information is most frequently requested
  • A testing environment for refining agent behaviour before production exposure

They are intentionally constrained: not all systems are exposed, and not all actions are permitted through chat. Instead, they operate under explicit permission boundaries defined by the underlying control structures.

items.title: Evolution Path
items.text:
The system is designed to evolve in stages:

  1. Internal assistant phase
  2. Restricted to partners and internal operations

  3. Focus on read-only queries and controlled updates

  4. Operational automation phase

  5. Integration with workflow execution (logging, updates, triggers)

  6. Expansion of structured commands beyond simple queries

  7. Customer-facing phase

  8. Selective exposure of chat agents to external users
  9. Limited to well-defined, high-confidence interactions
  10. Tight monitoring and refinement of response behaviour

Each stage builds on the reliability and constraints of the previous one rather than replacing it.

items.title: Operational Constraint
items.text:
Despite its accessibility, this layer remains governed by strict control rules:

  • Only predefined data sources and actions are accessible
  • Sensitive operations require explicit permission boundaries
  • Outputs are structured and deterministic wherever possible
  • Free-form generation is minimized in favour of system-backed responses

This ensures that the chat interface remains an operational tool rather than an uncontrolled conversational layer.

items.title: Orchestrated Agent Layer (Operational Workforce Substitution)
items.text:
This layer introduces structured, orchestrated AI agents designed to perform categories of work that a growing business would otherwise allocate to additional hires. The objective is not automation for its own sake, but the creation of a parallel operational workforce that executes repeatable, rules-based business functions with higher consistency, lower latency, and no linear headcount scaling.

Rather than acting as isolated tools, these agents operate as a coordinated system. Each agent has a defined domain, input sources, output constraints, and interaction rules. Together, they form an execution layer that sits between raw business systems and human decision-making.

The primary value is structural: as operational load increases, capacity is added through configuration rather than recruitment.

items.title: System Design Principle
items.text:
The system is built around a simple constraint model:

  • Humans define intent, priorities, and exceptions
  • Agents execute bounded operational work within defined domains
  • Structured data systems provide source-of-truth inputs
  • Outputs are standardised, traceable, and reusable

This creates a separation between decision-making, execution, and record-keeping, reducing cognitive and administrative load on operators.

Agents are not general assistants. They are role-scoped execution units embedded into business processes.

items.title: Candidate Agent Roles
items.text: Each role corresponds to a class of operational work that typically scales with staffing pressure in early and mid-stage businesses.

items.title: Sales Follow-Up Agent
items.text:
This agent manages continuity in the sales pipeline by handling structured communication patterns and routine engagement tasks.

Core functions include:

  • Monitoring inbound and warm leads across defined channels
  • Generating contextual follow-up messages based on prior interactions
  • Maintaining cadence for stalled or partially engaged prospects
  • Drafting check-ins that align with current pipeline state
  • Flagging opportunities requiring human intervention or escalation

The objective is not persuasion complexity, but consistency of pipeline motion, ensuring no opportunity decays due to attention gaps.

items.title: Reporting Agent
items.text:
This agent automates recurring analytical and operational reporting workflows across structured data sources.

Core functions include:

  • Aggregating data from Power BI, Excel, and other structured sources
  • Producing scheduled reports with consistent formatting and structure
  • Reconciling metrics across systems to reduce inconsistencies
  • Generating executive summaries for recurring operational review
  • Highlighting anomalies or deviations from expected baselines

This replaces manual compilation cycles and ensures reporting becomes a continuous system output rather than a periodic human task.

items.title: Catalogue & Inventory Agent
items.text:
This agent manages structured product or service catalogues across multiple input sources.

Core functions include:

  • Reconciling inventory data across suppliers or internal systems
  • Normalising inconsistent product or item representations
  • Detecting gaps, mismatches, or missing entries
  • Flagging low-stock or unaligned catalogue items
  • Maintaining a unified, queryable catalogue structure

This layer becomes critical when operational complexity increases across multiple supply streams or product variations.

items.title: Admin & Back-Office Agent
items.text:
This agent absorbs repetitive administrative workload that typically accumulates as operational overhead in growing organisations.

Core functions include:

  • Handling routine data entry and transformation tasks
  • Maintaining logs, structured notes, and operational records
  • Processing internal requests that follow predictable patterns
  • Supporting compliance-related documentation workflows
  • Reducing friction in day-to-day coordination tasks

The goal is to remove context-switch tax from human operators by delegating predictable administrative cycles.

items.title: System Backbone (Execution Environment)
items.text:
These agents are not standalone applications. They are embedded into a broader execution environment that defines how work is authored, versioned, and coordinated.

The backbone consists of:

  • Command-line and developer-adjacent tooling
  • VS Code and Cursor as primary execution environments

  • AI-assisted development workflows integrated directly into editing surfaces

  • Version control and traceability

  • Git and GitHub used as structural memory and audit layer

  • All agent outputs can be versioned, diffed, and reviewed

  • Cross-tool markdown system

  • Markdown acts as the universal interchange format
  • Enables consistent data flow between tools, agents, and human-readable systems

This backbone ensures that agents operate within a software-native operational environment, not as isolated conversational components.

items.title: Architectural Impact
items.text:
The introduction of orchestrated agents shifts the business structure in three key ways:

  • From headcount scaling to system scaling

  • Operational capacity increases through configuration rather than hiring

  • From manual execution to delegated workflows

  • Repetitive business processes become continuously running systems

  • From fragmented tools to unified execution layer

  • Sales, reporting, inventory, and admin workflows converge into a single coordinated system

items.title: Strategic Outcome
items.text:
As this layer matures, it forms a durable operational substrate for the business:

  • Routine workload is absorbed by role-specific agents
  • Human attention is preserved for exceptions, strategy, and relationship dynamics
  • Operational consistency increases as variance shifts from human execution to system design
  • The organisation becomes increasingly legible, traceable, and automatable over time

items.title: Entry-creator CLI Implementation Plan
items.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (- [ ]) syntax for tracking.

Goal: A local Python CLI that scaffolds a correctly-named, template-filled entry (challenge/meeting/timeline) and hands it to the editor, with an optional --fill mode that prompts each section at the terminal.

Architecture: One module scripts/new_entry.py = pure helpers (slug, collision, stamping, fill formatting) + an interactive main(). Pure helpers are unit-tested; the interactive shell gets a manual smoke test. A ./new-entry wrapper runs it via the venv.

Tech Stack: Python 3 (stdlib only — re, os, datetime, subprocess, unittest). No new dependencies. Runs from ./.venv.

items.title: Global Constraints
items.text:
• Module filename uses an underscore (scripts/new_entry.py) so tests can import it; the human-facing command is the ./new-entry wrapper. (Spec said new-entry.py; underscore chosen for importability.)
  • Section → folder map (6 types): Challenge→docs/business-challenges/, Meeting→docs/work/meetings/, Call→docs/work/calls/, Idea→docs/ideas/, Reference→docs/refs/, Timeline→docs/timeline/. Templates already exist in templates/ (challenge.md, meeting.md, call.md, idea.md, reference.md, timeline.md).
  • Slug: lowercase, non-[a-z0-9] runs → single -, trim leading/trailing -.
  • Filename <date>-<slug>.md; collisions append -TWO…-TEN to the file and (TWO)…(TEN) to the H1 only; 11th is an error.
  • Date default = system today (ISO YYYY-MM-DD).
  • This folder is not a git repo, so this plan omits git commit steps. At each checkpoint, run the full test suite instead. If you want history, run git init first, then commit after each task.
  • Run tests with: ./.venv/bin/python -m unittest scripts.test_new_entry -v (from repo root).

# scripts/new_entry.py
import os
import re

ORDINALS = {2: "TWO", 3: "THREE", 4: "FOUR", 5: "FIVE", 6: "SIX",
            7: "SEVEN", 8: "EIGHT", 9: "NINE", 10: "TEN"}

def slugify(title):
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", title.lower()).strip("-")

def resolve_collision(folder, date, slug):
    base = f"{date}-{slug}"
    first = os.path.join(folder, base + ".md")
    if not os.path.exists(first):
        return first, None
    for n in range(2, 11):
        word = ORDINALS[n]
        cand = os.path.join(folder, f"{base}-{word}.md")
        if not os.path.exists(cand):
            return cand, word
    raise SystemExit(f"error: more than ten '{base}' entries — check {folder}")

def stamp(template_text, title, date, suffix_word):
    h1 = title if not suffix_word else f"{title} ({suffix_word})"
    text = template_text.replace("YYYY-MM-DD", date)
    text = re.sub(r"(?m)^title:.*$", f"title: {title}", text, count=1)
    text = re.sub(r"(?m)^# .*$", f"# {h1} — {date}", text, count=1)
    return text

# append to scripts/new_entry.py
def section_shape(placeholder_body):
    s = placeholder_body.lstrip()
    if s.startswith("- [ ]"):
        return "task"
    if s.startswith("- "):
        return "list"
    return "prose"

def render_body(lines, shape):
    if shape == "task":
        return "\n".join(f"- [ ] {l}" for l in lines)
    if shape == "list":
        return "\n".join(f"- {l}" for l in lines)
    return "\n".join(lines)

def render_attendees(names):
    return "attendees: [" + ", ".join(names) + "]"

def render_tags(tags):
    return "tags:\n" + "\n".join(f"  - {t}" for t in tags)

Interfaces: - Consumes: slugify, resolve_collision, stamp, section_shape, render_body, render_attendees, render_tags from Tasks 1–2. - Produces: main(argv) entry point.

  • Step 1: Add the interactive shell
# append to scripts/new_entry.py
import sys
import subprocess
from datetime import date

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
SECTIONS = {
    "1": ("templates/challenge.md", "docs/business-challenges"),
    "2": ("templates/meeting.md",   "docs/work/meetings"),
    "3": ("templates/call.md",      "docs/work/calls"),
    "4": ("templates/idea.md",      "docs/ideas"),
    "5": ("templates/reference.md", "docs/refs"),
    "6": ("templates/timeline.md",  "docs/timeline"),
}

def ask(prompt, default=None):
    while True:
        val = input(prompt).strip()
        if val:
            return val
        if default is not None:
            return default
        print("  (required)")

def collect_lines(header):
    """One entry per line; a blank line finishes. Returns list[str]."""
    print(header)
    lines = []
    while True:
        val = input("  > ").rstrip("\n")
        if val == "":
            return lines
        lines.append(val)

def open_editor(path):
    for cmd in (["subl", path], [os.environ.get("EDITOR", ""), path], ["nano", path]):
        if not cmd[0]:
            continue
        try:
            subprocess.call(cmd)
            return True
        except FileNotFoundError:
            continue
    print(f"(no editor found — file written to {path})")
    return False

def main(argv):
    fill = "--fill" in argv
    print("Section?  [1] Challenge  [2] Meeting  [3] Call")
    print("          [4] Idea       [5] Reference  [6] Timeline")
    choice = ask("  > ")
    if choice not in SECTIONS:
        raise SystemExit("error: pick 1–6")
    tpl_rel, folder_rel = SECTIONS[choice]
    title = ask("Title  > ")
    today = date.today().isoformat()
    entry_date = ask(f"Date [{today}]  > ", default=today)

    text = open(os.path.join(ROOT, tpl_rel), encoding="utf-8").read()
    folder = os.path.join(ROOT, folder_rel)
    path, suffix = resolve_collision(folder, entry_date, slugify(title))
    text = stamp(text, title, entry_date, suffix)

    if fill:
        text = run_fill(text)

    os.makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text if text.endswith("\n") else text + "\n")
    print(f"✔ wrote {os.path.relpath(path, ROOT)}")
    open_editor(path)

def run_fill(text):
    # Front-matter lists first.
    if re.search(r"(?m)^attendees:", text):
        names = collect_lines("Attendees (one name per line — empty line when done)")
        if names:
            text = re.sub(r"(?m)^attendees:.*$", render_attendees(names), text, count=1)
    if re.search(r"(?m)^tags:", text):
        tags = collect_lines("Tags (one per line — empty line when done)")
        if tags:
            text = re.sub(r"(?m)^tags:\n(?:\s*-.*\n?)*", render_tags(tags) + "\n", text, count=1)
    # Then each ## section body.
    parts = re.split(r"(?m)^(## .+)$", text)
    rebuilt = parts[0]
    for i in range(1, len(parts), 2):
        heading = parts[i]
        body = parts[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(parts) else "\n"
        shape = section_shape(body.strip("\n"))
        hint = {"task": "one per line", "list": "one bullet per line",
                "prose": "type freely"}[shape]
        lines = collect_lines(f"{heading}  ({hint} — empty line when done)")
        if lines:
            rebuilt += heading + "\n\n" + render_body(lines, shape) + "\n\n"
        else:
            rebuilt += heading + body
    return rebuilt

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1:])

items.title: Notes for the implementer
items.text:
• Learning-mode contribution points: slugify() and the ORDINALS map encode taste calls (how hard to strip punctuation, how far the word-form ladder goes). Reference implementations are given above; the human may want to substitute their own — check with them before finalizing these two.
  • The run_fill tag regex assumes the template's tags: block is contiguous - lines (true for templates/timeline.md). If a template's front matter changes shape, revisit that substitution.

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
Collapse the current authoring recipe from WORKFLOWS FOR Project Hub Site (cp templates/… → rename with date → $EDITOR) into a single command that scaffolds a correctly-named, template-filled entry and hands it off for writing. No hand-typed filenames or dates.

Scope is local CLI only. The browser form (File System Access API) is explicitly parked as a future sub-project and is out of scope here.

items.title: Where it lives
items.text:
scripts/new-entry.py, run from the repo root via the existing venv:

python3 scripts/new-entry.py            # scaffold mode (default)
python3 scripts/new-entry.py --fill     # fill mode

A thin executable wrapper ./new-entry (calls ./.venv/bin/python scripts/new-entry.py "$@") is added for ergonomics, mirroring ./build.sh.

Python is chosen to match scripts/gen-blog-nav.py (same venv, same string/front-matter handling) and to keep the slug + collision logic clean.

items.title: Section → template → destination
items.text:
A fixed map, matching the current repo layout:

Section (prompt) Template Destination folder Body sections [1] Challenge templates/challenge.md docs/business-challenges/ The issue · How we see it · What we've tried · Shape of a solution · Technical preferences · Company implications · Strategic commentary (unchanged 7-section template) [2] Meeting templates/meeting.md docs/work/meetings/ Agenda · Decisions · Action items · Actions taken (+ attendees: front matter) [3] Call templates/call.md docs/work/calls/ Topics · Observations · Insights · Suggested actions [4] Idea templates/idea.md docs/ideas/ Topic · Summary · Connections · Contexts [5] Reference templates/reference.md docs/refs/ Description · Link (title = the entry's H1, not a separate section) [6] Timeline templates/timeline.md docs/timeline/ single prose body (unchanged) [7] Automation templates/automation.md docs/automations/ Overview · Trigger · Steps · Systems & tools · Intended impact · Business considerations [8] Operation templates/operation.md docs/operations/ Business area · Current approach · AI & agent enhancement · Depth & reach gained · Considerations

Nav wiring status: all eight sections are wired into gen-blog-nav.py (BLOG_SECTIONS) + zensical.toml marker pairs and verified with a build. Ideas and References were converted to auto-generated blog sections — each folder's former intro page was promoted to index.md (the landing), with ideas/ also keeping automation-inventory.md as an entry.

items.title: Inputs (interactive, one prompt at a time)
items.text:
Section?  [1] Challenge  [2] Meeting     [3] Call
          [4] Idea       [5] Reference   [6] Timeline
          [7] Automation [8] Operation   > 1
Title     > Supplier onboarding is slow
Date [2026-07-05] >              ← Enter accepts today (system date)
  • Section — required; accepts the digit or a case-insensitive name.
  • Title — required; free text, used verbatim for the H1 and slugified for the filename.
  • Date — defaults to today (date.today().isoformat()); Enter accepts, or type an ISO YYYY-MM-DD. Invalid input re-prompts.

items.title: The shared engine (both modes)
items.text:
1. Load the section's template file.
  2. Slugify the title: lowercase → strip to [a-z0-9] and spaces → spaces to hyphens → collapse repeated hyphens → trim leading/trailing hyphens. "Supplier onboarding is slow" → supplier-onboarding-is-slow.
  3. Stamp placeholders into the template text (robust to which placeholder word each template uses):
  4. every literal YYYY-MM-DD → the chosen date;
  5. the front-matter title: value → the real title;
  6. the H1 is rebuilt as # {title} — {date}.
  7. Resolve collisions (see below) to get the final path.
  8. Write the file (utf-8, newline-terminated).

items.title: Two modes
items.text:
• Scaffold (default). Run the engine, write the file, then hand off to the editor: try subl -w/subl, else $EDITOR, else nano. You write the prose in the editor. This is the everyday path.
  • Fill (--fill). Before writing, prompt for the front-matter list fields (see below), then walk the template's ## section headings in order, prompting for each body. After filling, the file is written; the editor is then opened too so you can revise (same handoff as scaffold).

items.title: Fill-mode input mechanic
items.text:
Plain Enter only — no Ctrl/modifier keys (terminals can't reliably see Ctrl+Enter). Within any section:

  • Enter after typing text commits that line and stays in the section for the next line.
  • Enter on an empty line finishes the section and advances to the next prompt.

So "next bullet" and "next prompt" are the same key; the difference is whether you typed anything first. An empty section (empty line straight away) keeps the template's placeholder hint text.

items.title: List sections vs. prose sections
items.text:
The template decides which shape a section is — the tool does not hardcode it:

  • A ## section whose placeholder body starts with - is a list section (Agenda, Decisions): the tool prints the - marker and each line you type becomes a bullet. - [ ] placeholders (Action items) keep the checkbox marker.
  • Any other ## section is prose (the challenge template's seven sections; the timeline template's single body under the H1, which has no ## headings): each line you type is kept verbatim.

Known limitation: because an empty line ends a section, prose sections cannot contain a blank line, so no multi-paragraph prose in fill mode. The editor opens immediately afterward for anything longer.

items.title: Front-matter list fields (prompted in fill mode)
items.text:
• Meeting attendees: — prompted one name per line, written back in the template's flow style: attendees: [Morgen, Priya].
  • Timeline tags: — prompted one tag per line, written back in the template's block style (tags: then - Foundation lines).

These use the same one-per-line, empty-line-to-finish mechanic as list sections.

items.title: Collision handling
items.text:
If the computed <date>-<slug>.md already exists in the destination, append a word-form ordinal and retry, first free wins:

2026-07-05-standup.md          (first)
2026-07-05-standup-TWO.md      (second)
2026-07-05-standup-THREE.md    (third)   … -FOUR, -FIVE, …

When a suffix is applied, the H1 also gets a matching parenthetical so the generated nav (labels come from each page's H1) self-distinguishes:

# Standup — 2026-07-05          (first)
# Standup (TWO) — 2026-07-05    (second)

The tool prints the final filename it landed on. The number→word map is defined explicitly for TWO through TEN; hitting an 11th same-day, same-title entry is an error (clear message, non-zero exit) rather than a silent fallback — that many collisions means something is wrong upstream.

items.title: Nav is out of scope
items.text: The tool only places a correctly-named file in the right folder. The left-nav ordering is owned by scripts/gen-blog-nav.py, which runs inside ./build.sh (and edits zensical.toml). Running the nav generator or zensical.toml edits are deliberately not this tool's job — dropping the file is the whole contract, exactly as the existing folder-driven design assumes.

items.title: Error handling
items.text:
• Missing/blank required input → re-prompt (does not crash).
  • Unwritable destination or missing template → clear error, non-zero exit, no partial file left behind.
  • Editor not found (no subl, $EDITOR, or nano) → still write the file and print its path so nothing is lost; report that no editor could be launched.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
Pure-function core is unit-tested without touching the real docs/ tree:

  • slugify — spaces, punctuation, casing, unicode, repeated/edge hyphens.
  • collision suffixing — first-free selection and the word-form sequence, including the H1 parenthetical.
  • placeholder stamping — date + title land in front matter and H1 for each of the three templates.
  • section-shape detection — - / - [ ] placeholders classify as list sections (correct marker emitted), everything else as prose; attendees/tags render in each template's respective front-matter style.

Collision and I/O tests run against a tmp_path fixture, not docs/.

items.title: Out of scope (parked)
items.text:
• The on-site browser form (File System Access API path) — future sub-project 2.
  • Any write to zensical.toml; encryption/deploy; nav regeneration.
  • Reconciling index.md / the catalogue example to the 7-section template (the separate "drift" cleanup) — unrelated to this tool.
